issue_title: Compatibility reconsideration: defaulted discriminator fields prevent validation of explicitly tagged commands
issue_body:
Reproduction [repository](https://github.com/david-gettins/zod-issue-repro) link.

We are affected in production by the behaviour discussed in #6545. I understand that rejecting overlapping discriminator inputs is intentional; this is a request to reconsider the compatibility impact on applications that reuse concrete construction schemas in discriminated unions.

We use defaulted literal type fields when constructing a known command or event. For example, `CreateUser.parse(...)` supplies "CreateUser" because the caller has already selected the concrete schema.

We then use the discriminated union to validate explicitly tagged messages. We are not asking it to infer a command kind from an omitted discriminator. The problem is that the overlap on undefined prevents validation even when the input already contains a unique, explicit tag.

## Proposal

Could Zod support this composition pattern while continuing to reject ambiguous untagged input?

Our required behaviour is that explicit, unique discriminator values continue to select and validate their corresponding members. Duplicate explicit literal tags could remain schema-definition errors.

We understand that this would relax the current schema-wide uniqueness rule. We are asking whether preserving this existing construction-and-validation pattern warrants that exception, or whether an explicit compatibility option would be acceptable.

We have identified the safeExtend/unwrap workaround. It preserves concrete-schema construction defaults, but requires migration and regression testing at the affected union composition sites.

issue_title: Excessive memory retention in v4 memoizer
issue_body:
We are seeing a severe memory regression after upgrading Zod from 4.4.3 to 4.5.4 in a large Backstage monorepo.

The workload is a repository-wide ESLint run:

```sh
yarn eslint . --no-cache
```

With Zod 4.4.3 it completes normally:

```text
Elapsed time: 49.16s
Maximum RSS: 5,487,520 KB
Exit status: 0
```

With Zod 4.5.4, even with an 8 GiB limit, it eventually runs out of memory:

```text
Elapsed time before OOM: 181.32s
Maximum RSS before OOM: 8,723,528 KB
Exit status: 1
```

The final GC cycles look like this:

```text
Mark-Compact 8042.9 (8224.5) -> 8027.5 (8225.2) MB
Mark-Compact 8043.5 (8225.2) -> 8028.1 (8225.7) MB

FATAL ERROR: Ineffective mark-compacts near heap limit
Allocation failed - JavaScript heap out of memory
```

I traced the regression to the `lastCtx` / `lastBucket` cache in `src/v4/core/memoizer.ts`.

Current code:

```ts

let lastBucket: Map<object, Entry> | undefined;

// ...

let bucket: Map<object, Entry>;

if (lastCtx === ctx) {
  bucket = lastBucket!;
} else {
  bucket = bucketFor(state, inst);
  lastCtx = ctx;
  lastBucket = bucket;
}
```

Removing this additional cache and always retrieving the bucket from the parse state fixes the problem:

```

With that change applied to Zod 4.5.4:

```text
Elapsed time: 48.44s
Maximum RSS: 5,621,244 KB
Exit status: 0
```

Here are teh results:

| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 4.4.3 | success | 49.16s | 5,487,520 KB |
| 4.5.4 | OOM | 181.32s | 8,723,528 KB |

pr_title: fix(v4): stop the memoizer from pinning a finished parse
pr_body:
Fixes #6557.

A recursive schema held the entire input and output graph of its last parse until the next parse replaced it. The memoizer caches the current parse context and its bucket on the schema instance, so a re-entered container skips a lookup — but nothing ever clears that slot, and it outlives the parse. One long-lived schema therefore pinned every object the parse touched, across every schema in it. Reported as an 8 GiB OOM on a repo-wide ESLint run that completed on 4.4.3.

The buckets only ever need `get` and `set`, and the back-edge set only needs `add` and `has`. Making the parse state weak throughout leaves the fast path exactly as it is and lets the graph go.

| --- | ---: | ---: |

| bundle, mini | 3710 B gz | 3710 B gz |

issue_title: `z.compile`: a runtime island leaks one indent level into the rest of the generated source, leading to substantial memory overhead
pr_title: fix(compile): unwind the doc indent when a child generator throws
pr_body:
`Doc.indented` decremented the indent level after the callback returned, so a child generator that threw left it raised. `compileChild` catches `ZodCompileUnsupportedError`, rolls back the emitted content and the constant/var counters, and emits a runtime island instead — but the indent was never part of that rollback. Every line after an island got written one level deeper, and each further island added another, so a schema with N islands emitted O(N²) leading spaces. Nothing reads that whitespace, but `new Function` retains the source, so it is live memory.

Moving the decrement into a `finally` is the whole fix. It belongs in `Doc` rather than at the call site: the throw unwinds through whichever `indented` frames it was under, so the ~30 call sites in `compile.ts` would each need the same wrapper otherwise.

On a 162-branch discriminated union with 324 `z.coerce.number()` islands:

| | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| generated source | 976 KB (90% whitespace) | 103 KB (4.6%) |
| retained heap per compiled fn | 1.01 MB | 162 KB |
| `compileFn` | 4.8 ms | 3.9 ms |

Dedented, the generated code is character-identical before and after, so nothing on the parse path moves. Bundle cost is +10 gzipped bytes on a classic `z.object` fixture, and zero on the mini fixtures and the classic string/boolean ones.

The source and retained-heap figures come from [`packages/bench/memory/indent-leak.ts`](https://github.com/colinhacks/zod/blob/main/packages/bench/memory/indent-leak.ts), which restores the pre-fix `indented` onto the prototype so the comparison stays runnable. The commit message carries an earlier, lower pair for retained heap: that measurement compiled one schema repeatedly, and V8's compilation cache shares generated source between byte-identical compiles.

Reported with a working branch by @aaronhipple.

Closes #6561

issue_title: `toJSONSchema()`: chaining `.int()` after `.min()`/`.max()` replaces explicit bounds

pr_body:

pr_title: fix(v4): parse recursive schemas built by a factory
pr_body:
Fixes #6526.

A recursive schema built by a factory throws `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` on 4.5.x, after about eight seconds on the main thread. It parsed fine on 4.4.3. Published schemas hit it — `zod-geojson` builds its geometry schemas this way, so an empty feature collection crashes.

```ts
const Node = (): any =>
  z.object({
    id: z.number(),
    get child() {
      return z.array(Node()); // a fresh instance on every read
    },
  });

z.object({ root: Node() }).parse({ root: { id: 1, child: [] } }); // RangeError
```

The cycle walk added in #6387 decides whether a parse can re-enter the same schema, so the memoizer can detach when no cycle is possible. Instance identity is the only thing that terminates that walk: it marks what it enters and stops when it meets a mark. A factory returns a new instance per call, so resolving one getter mints a whole new subtree, the walk never revisits a node, and it constructs schemas until the stack runs out. Descent at parse time was always data-directed and therefore finite, which is why 4.4.3 was unaffected.

The walk no longer resolves anything that runs user code, and reports a cycle for every edge it therefore cannot follow — a shape getter, or a `z.lazy` nobody has resolved. That terminates by construction and needs no depth limit. It errs in one direction only: it can report a cycle that does not exist, never the reverse. The same rule already governs `compile.ts`, which treats "can't tell" as recursive.

The first parse resolves the getters along its path and `z.lazy` stores its inner type on the def, and one recheck then reads plain values and answers exactly. issue_title: fromJSONSchema silently ignores minProperties and maxProperties
issue_body:
## `fromJSONSchema` silently ignores `minProperties` and `maxProperties`

Both keywords are listed in `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` in `from-json-schema.ts` (so they are silently consumed instead of falling into `extraMeta`), but no validation logic is ever attached to the resulting schema. An object with `minProperties: 1` accepts `{}`, and one with `maxProperties: 2` accepts three or more keys without error.

### Reproduce

```ts
import { fromJSONSchema } from "zod/v4";

const schema = fromJSONSchema({
  type: "object",
  properties: { a: { type: "string" }, b: { type: "number" } },
  minProperties: 1,
  maxProperties: 2,
});

schema.safeParse({}).success      // true  — should be false (0 < minProperties)
schema.safeParse({ a: "x", b: 1, c: true }).success  // true  — should be false (3 > maxProperties)
```

### Expected

Both should fail: `{}` has 0 properties (< `minProperties: 1`), and `{ a, b, c }` has 3 properties (> `maxProperties: 2`).

### Actual

Both parse successfully — the keywords are consumed without effect.

### Root cause

`minProperties` and `maxProperties` appear in the `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` set (lines 62–63 of `from-json-schema.ts`) but are never referenced in `convertBaseSchema` or `convertSchema`. By contrast, the analogous array keywords `minItems`/`maxItems` are applied via `.check(z.minLength(...))` / `.check(z.maxLength(...))`, and string `minLength`/`maxLength` via `.min()` / `.max()`. The object property-count keywords simply have no corresponding branch.

### Fix

Layer a `.check()` on the object schema after `propertyNames` handling, counting `Object.keys(value).length` against the threshold and emitting `too_small` / `too_big` issues with `origin: "object"`. I have a patch ready (37 lines in `from-json-schema.ts` + 40 lines of regression tests in `from-json-schema.test.ts`) — happy to open a PR if `pull_request_creation_policy` allows, or I can attach the diff here.
pr_title: fix(v4): enforce the six JSON Schema keywords fromJSONSchema silently dropped
pr_body:
`fromJSONSchema` lists six validation keywords in `RECOGNIZED_KEYS` and silently drops them: `minProperties`, `maxProperties`, `uniqueItems`, `contains`, `minContains`, `maxContains`. A converted schema accepts data the source schema rejects, which is the worst failure mode for a validating converter — the file already throws for `not` and `if/then/else` rather than ignoring them.

```ts
const schema = z.fromJSONSchema({ type: "object", minProperties: 1 });
schema.safeParse({}).success; // main: true — now false
```

All six are now enforced inside the converter, with no new public API — nothing to undo when the @zod/json push happens. The property counts fold into the pre-pipe guard that already enforces `propertyNames`, so they see the raw input: a key synthesized by a property `default` does not satisfy `minProperties`, and a dropped `__proto__` still counts, matching how JSON Schema validators see the instance. `uniqueItems` and the `contains` family run as checks on the converted array schema, with structural equality (two objects with the same entries in different key order are duplicates). Each keyword is also carried into metadata the way `propertyNames` already is, so `toJSONSchema` round-trips all of them.

issue_title: z.emoji() accepts strings that contain no emoji
issue_body:
### Problem

`z.emoji()` accepts strings that contain no emoji at all:

```ts
z.emoji().parse("123");        // passes
z.emoji().parse("#");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("*");          // passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{200D}");   // lone ZWJ, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{FE0F}");   // lone variation selector, passes
z.emoji().parse("\u{1F3FD}");  // lone skin tone modifier, passes
```

The pattern is `^[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Emoji_Component}]+$`. `\p{Emoji_Component}` is not a set of emoji — it is the set of pieces that combine with one: ASCII digits `0`–`9`, `#`, `*`, regional indicators, skin tone modifiers, ZWJ and variation selectors. A string built only from components is not an emoji.

### Suggested fix

Keep the character class exactly as it is — the single class matters, #6347 replaced an alternation with it to kill the exponential backtracking over the U+1F9B0–U+1F9B3 overlap — and add a leading lookahead requiring one anchor: an `Extended_Pictographic`, a regional indicator, or U+20E3, the enclosing keycap that makes `1️⃣` an emoji.

```
^(?=[\s\S]*[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Regional_Indicator}⃣])[\p{Extended_Pictographic}\p{Emoji_Component}]+$
```

`[\s\S]` rather than `[^]`, and `⃣` rather than `\u{20E3}`, because the pattern is emitted into JSON Schema and not every consumer parses the ECMAScript-only spellings.

### Checks

- every emoji in `unicode-emoji-json` (1914 entries) still validates, and every existing fixture in `string.test.ts` passes, keycap sequences included
- `recheck` reports the new pattern safe; the lookahead is a single unnested quantifier, so matching stays linear — measured at 1k/10k/50k characters, on both the matching and the failing path, it costs about 10% more than the current pattern and scales linearly
- two snapshots that carry the pattern as text need updating
- full `packages/zod` suite passes (7835 tests)

Implemented on a branch with tests for the component-only cases above. The change is here, ready

pr_title: fix(v4): fold an intersection of object schemas into one object
pr_body:
Converting an intersection produces `allOf: [A, B]`. In JSON Schema, `additionalProperties` only sees `properties` in its own schema object — never a sibling `allOf` entry — so two closed object members forbid each other's keys and no object validates, while the parser accepts the same value.

```ts
const schema = z.object({ name: z.string() }).and(z.object({ age: z.number() }));

schema.parse({ name: "a", age: 1 }); // ok
// the emitted schema rejects that, and every other object too
```

The parser already answers this. Its intersection handler pools the members' key sets: a key is reported as unrecognized only when *every* side rejects it. So an intersection is closed exactly when every member is closed, over the union of their keys — which is a single object, and is what the intersection means.

```json
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" }, "age": { "type": "number" } },

pr_body:
Exports `z.withParser(schema, parser)` — the installer half of `compile()`, so a build-time or native compiler can supply the parser where `new Function` isn't available. `compile()` calls it, so the wrapper contract has one implementation.

The parser returns the parsed value or `INVALID`, which is now exported too. Zod keeps everything else: the clone, the async/backward/skip-check bypasses, the memoizer back-edge check, the fallback flag, and the runtime as the only source of `ZodError`s.

Two design calls worth flagging.

A supplied parser is its own validator rather than getting a generated assert-only one. Reaching `compileValidator` pulls `compileFn` and the whole codegen into any bundle that imports `withParser` — measured at +7.4 KB gz on a classic fixture. It's also the better semantic: one implementation means `parse()` and `validate()` can't disagree, and an undefined `definite` keeps `validate`'s runtime re-parse on every rejection.

The recursion guard moves with the installer. A supplied parser skips `compileFn`, which is what refuses a schema whose subtree contains a cycle; generated code never receives the parse context, so only the runtime can close one. `isRecursiveSchema` needs no eval, so it runs on this path too.

The email regex opened with `(?!\.)(?!.*\.\.)`, and the second lookahead scanned the whole string before the match started. Both are gone:

```

The `(?:seg\.)*seg` form says that structurally, so the accepted language is unchanged, and the grammar is the one in the compile work's open-levers note. Equivalence here is exhaustive rather than sampled: both forms are built only from character classes, so a string's verdict depends only on which classes each of its characters falls in, and exactly nine distinct signatures occur across the whole character space. Every string up to length 8 over a nine-symbol alphabet covering those signatures agrees — 19.2M of them — plus 122M more up to length 11 over two subsets. pr_title: perf(v4): settle z.validate on the first failure in parse order
pr_body:
Today `z.validate()` walks the whole schema even after the answer is settled. On a 20-key object with a wrong value in the first key, it still parses the other 19 — the boolean was decided at key 0, and everything after it is work nobody reads.

This gives the runtime parse path an early exit and lets `validate` / `validateAsync` take it. Nothing else does, and there is no new public surface: the context field is internal, and the commented-out `abortEarly` on the public `ParseContext` stays commented out.

The asymmetry is what makes it safe. Reporting every issue and handing back a well-formed value is what `safeParse` owes its caller, so it can never stop early. A boolean is all `validate` returns, so the truncated value a stopped container leaves behind is never read by anyone.

### The contract

First failure in parse order wins. Once an aborting issue settles the boolean, the container stops before the next child it would have parsed, so a callback there never runs — exactly as if it were not in the schema:

```ts
const schema = z.object({
  a: z.number(),
  b: z.string().transform(() => { throw new RangeError(); }),
});
schema.safeParse({ a: "bad", b: "ok" }); // throws: it walks the whole shape
z.validate(schema,  { a: "bad", b: "ok" }); // false: `a` settled it, `b` never ran
```

A throw that does happen still bubbles, unchanged. Nothing rejects before the callback below, so `validate` runs it and the exception is the caller's:

```ts
z.validate(z.object({ a: z.string().transform(boom), b: z.number() }), { a: "ok", b: "bad" }); // throws
```

The stop lands between children, never inside one. A map entry parses its key and value together, and a tuple runs every fixed item before `handleTupleResults` decides which issues survive — so neither can skip the other half, and both stay at `safeParse` parity. Stopping inside them would risk a discarded issue turning a `false` into a `true`, which is not worth the few nanoseconds. A test pins both.

pr_body:
`z.validate` on a compiled schema re-ran the entire schema through the interpreter whenever the compiled validator rejected, just to reach the verdict the fast path had already produced.

Often that second pass is dead work, because the compiled `INVALID` already means the runtime would reject — which is why a union can read a branch's `INVALID` as a rejection. Codegen now tracks a `definite` flag and `validate` skips the interpreted pass only while it survives. A call that passes a parse context still takes the interpreted path, since a context can change the verdict.

Two things clear the flag. Any hoisted **user callback** — a refine, transform, custom predicate, catch value or lazy getter — clears it, because that callback can throw and generated code can reject an earlier sibling before ever reaching it, so the rejection is no longer proof that the interpreter would have rejected rather than thrown. A **runtime island**, an **intersection**, and a **record key whose own compile is not definite** clear it directly. User code reaches generated code through a single `addUserConstant` helper that clears the flag, so a generator added later cannot quietly miss it.

What keeps the fast path is the callback-free subset: type, range and format checks, enums, literals, unions, and object, array and tuple members. That is the shape a type guard is usually asked about.

Compiled parsing semantics are untouched. The transform case is why this is a flag rather than a throw in generated code: a transform handing back a thenable has to keep answering `INVALID`, because the interpreter's own union falls through to the next branch there instead of propagating, and `compile-differential` pins that.

pr_body:
### Description

Written by an AI agent (Claude Code) on behalf of @ShreeBohara, who has reviewed it.

Resolves #11071

`toMatchObject` compares with `subsetEquality`, which is directional — it asks whether its second argument is contained in its first. That tester was forwarded into any asymmetric matcher found in the expected value.

`ArrayContaining` compares its sample as the left-hand side ([`equals(item, another, customTesters)`](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/blob/main/packages/expect/src/jest-asymmetric-matchers.ts#L212)), so the sample became the "object" and the actual element the "subset". Every field the sample declared beyond those present on the actual element was ignored:

```js
// passed before this change
expect({ records: [{ id: 1 }] }).toMatchObject({
  records: expect.arrayContaining([{ id: 1, required: 'x' }]),
})
```

The fix filters subset testers out where they are handed to a matcher, in `asymmetricMatch`. One detail made this less obvious than it looks: the contextual testers `subsetEquality` spawns for circular-reference tracking are fresh closures rather than the exported function, so filtering by `tester !== subsetEquality` alone does not remove them. They are registered as they are created and matched by identity.

Doing it in `asymmetricMatch` rather than at the `subsetEquality` recursion covers the case where the matcher is the root expected value and the exported `subsetEquality` arrives directly from `toMatchObject`:

```js

  expect.arrayContaining([{ id: 1, required: 'x' }]),
)
```

Testers that are not subset testers still reach matchers, so `iterableEquality` and the `toStrictEqual` testers behave as before — the existing `asymmetric matchers and equality testers` test covers that and still passes.

issue_title: jsdom environment turns every Blob/File request body into the string "undefined"
issue_body:
### Describe the bug

Under `environment: 'jsdom'`, a `Blob` or `File` used as a request body arrives as the literal string `undefined`. Nothing throws, so a test uploading a file passes while sending nine bytes of ASCII instead of its content.

```ts
const blob = new Blob(['hello world'], { type: 'text/plain' })
const text = await new Request('http://x.test/', { method: 'POST', body: blob }).text()
```

| environment | `text` |
| --- | --- |
| node | `"hello world"` |
| happy-dom | `"hello world"` |
| jsdom | `"undefined"` |

Same for a `File` inside `FormData`: the multipart part body is `undefined`, and `fetch(URL.createObjectURL(blob))` returns `undefined` too.

### Cause

`makeCompatBlob` in `packages/vitest/src/integrations/env/jsdom.ts` bridges jsdom's `Blob` to Node's `fetch` by reading a private field:

```ts
const buffer = (blob as any)[implSymbol]._buffer
return new NodeBlob_([buffer], { type: blob.type })
```

jsdom 28.0.0 renamed that field to `_bytes`, so the read is `undefined` and `new Blob([undefined])` stringifies it.

| jsdom | impl keys |
| --- | --- |
| 24.1.3 – 27.4.0 | `_buffer,_globalObject,type` |
| 28.1.0 – 29.1.1 | `_globalObject,type,_bytes` |

issue_body:
### Describe the bug

Skipping one test hides every obsolete snapshot in that file. With `update: 'none'`, the CI default, the run passes. With `-u`, the stale entries are never deleted.

`markSnapshotsAsCheckedForTest` in `packages/snapshot/src/port/state.ts` runs once per skipped test so the skipped test's own snapshots are not flagged as obsolete. This came in with ac9ba151d (#7126), which replaced `keyToTestName(key) === testName` with the regex so `toMatchSnapshot('name')` keys are covered, and dropped the prefix check along the way.

issue_body:
### Describe the bug

When a module is mocked with `vi.mock(import('...'), { spy: true })` and `mockReset: true` is configured, the automatic mock reset that runs before every test throws:

```
TypeError: Cyclic __proto__ value
    at Object.setPrototypeOf (<anonymous>)
    at reparentMockPrototype (.../vitest/dist/chunks/spy.*.js)
    at updateMockPrototype (.../vitest/dist/chunks/spy.*.js)
    at glob.mockReset (.../vitest/dist/chunks/spy.*.js)
    at resetAllMocks (.../vitest/dist/chunks/spy.*.js)
    at Object.resetAllMocks (.../vitest/dist/chunks/index.*.js)
    at clearModuleMocks (.../vitest/dist/chunks/index.*.js)
    at TestRunner.onBeforeTryTask (.../vitest/dist/chunks/index.*.js)
```

This reproduces even for the very first test in a file, because `mockReset` is applied before every test (including the first), and ends up calling `Object.setPrototypeOf(mock.prototype, mock.prototype)` on the spied module namespace object, which throws because it would create a cyclic prototype chain.

issue_body:
## Bug Description

In 5.0.0, importing from `vitest/config` and running `tsc` with `skipLibCheck: false` fails with
two errors that come from **vitest's own bundled `.d.ts` files**, not from user code:

```
node_modules/vitest/config.d.ts(2,21): error TS2307: Cannot find module '@vitest/expect' or its corresponding type declarations.
node_modules/vitest/dist/chunks/plugin.d.BbcoZhuj.d.ts(11,39): error TS2305: Module '"vitest/browser"' has no exported member 'MarkOptions'.
```

Both are dangling references to things a consumer never has:

1. **`@vitest/expect`** — `vitest/config.d.ts` line 2 does `import type {} from '@vitest/expect'`,
   but `@vitest/expect` is declared only in vitest's **devDependencies** (not `dependencies` or
   `peerDependencies`), so it is never installed in a consumer's tree. `npm ls @vitest/expect` in a
   fresh `npm i vitest@5` project prints `(empty)`. The 5.0 migration inlined `@vitest/expect`
   at runtime — this looks like a type-side import that was missed.

2. **`MarkOptions`** — `vitest/dist/chunks/plugin.d.*.d.ts` does
   `import { CDPSession, BrowserCommands, MarkOptions } from 'vitest/browser'`, but `vitest/browser`
   does not export `MarkOptions`. This is the same class of problem as #8662 (`BrowserCommands` from
   `vitest/browser`), fixed by #8666 — so `MarkOptions` looks like a **regression / missed member**
   of that fix.

**Expected:** vitest's published types type-check standalone (as on 4.x), so no errors.
**Actual:** the two errors above. `skipLibCheck: true` makes them disappear, confirming both come
from vitest's declaration files. Reproduces under both `moduleResolution: "bundler"` and `"nodenext"`,
and with TypeScript 5.x and 6.x.

Suggested fix:
1. Remove the leftover `import type {} from '@vitest/expect'` from `vitest/config.d.ts` (or move
   `@vitest/expect` to `dependencies`).
2. Export `MarkOptions` from `vitest/browser` (as #8666 did for `BrowserCommands`).

pr_title: perf(cache): hash the environment-invariant part of the fs module cache key once
pr_body:
### Description

`FileSystemModuleCache.generateCachePath()` builds every module's cache key by concatenating the serialized environment config (`cacheConfig` — which embeds the *contents* of every `configFileDependencies` file, plugin names, `resolve`, etc.) with the module id + source, and SHA-1s the whole string **per module**. On a large suite the invariant part dwarfs the module: in our case (~6k test files, ~30k modules transformed on a cold `experimental.fsModuleCache`) `cacheConfig` is ~100 KB, so the main thread hashes ~3 GB of identical bytes per cold run (~15 s of self time in a CPU profile of the main process, which is the bottleneck for vm-pool runs).

This hashes `NODE_ENV + version + cacheConfig` once per environment (memoized in the existing `fsEnvironmentHashMap`) and appends the 40-char digest to the per-module key material instead. Keys remain a pure function of exactly the same inputs; the only observable effect is that existing cache directories are not reused once after upgrading (the digest changes the key material), same as after any config change.

No new tests: behaviour is covered by `test/e2e/test/caching.test.ts` and `test/e2e/test/fs-module-cache-resiliency.test.ts` (both pass locally: 7/7). `eslint` clean on the file; `pnpm typecheck` shows the same pre-existing errors as `main` (unbuilt sibling packages), none in `packages/vitest`.

### What runtime/platform is your app running on? (with version if possible)

Reproduced on all three, same result: Node.js 26 (`@hono/node-server`), Bun 1.4.3, Deno 2.9.6.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

Reading the body as text first, then parsing it as form data, throws.

```ts
import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()

app.post('/', async (c) => {
  const raw = await c.req.text() // read the raw body first, e.g. to verify a signature
  const form = await c.req.formData() // throws here
  return c.json({ foo: form.get('foo') })

import { Hono } from 'hono'

const app = new Hono()
app.post('/', async (c) => {
  await c.req.text()
  return c.json({ foo: (await c.req.formData()).get('foo') })
})

await app.request('/', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'content-type': 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' },
  body: 'foo=bar',
})

`c.req.formData()` should return the parsed form, the same as when it is the first call. The body is already cached, so reading it a second way should still work.

issue_title: AWS Lambda streamHandle ignores writable backpressure and resolves before the response finishes
pr_title: fix(aws-lambda): respect backpressure when streaming the response body
pr_body:
Fixes #5333.

## Problem

`streamToNodeStream` in the AWS Lambda adapter ignored the return value of `writer.write()`:

```ts
while (!readResult.done) {
  writer.write(readResult.value)
  readResult = await reader.read()
}
writer.end()
```

Two consequences:

1. **No backpressure.** Once the response exceeds the destination's `highWaterMark`, `write()` returns `false`, but the loop keeps reading and writing. The whole body accumulates in the writable's internal buffer.
2. **Resolves too early.** `writer.end()` only signals that no more data is coming — it does not mean the stream has finished. `streamHandle` could resolve while `responseStream.writableFinished` was still `false`, so a Lambda invocation could complete before the response had actually been delivered.

## Fix

Read the body through an async generator and hand it to `pipeline` from `node:stream/promises`. `pipeline` paces reads against the destination, waits for `finish`, and propagates errors from either side — which is the behaviour the issue asks for, without hand-rolling the stream lifecycle.

`node:` imports are already used elsewhere in the Lambda adapters (`src/adapter/lambda-edge/handler.ts` imports `node:crypto`), and `stream/promises` is available on every Node version that supports Lambda response streaming.

## Tests

`runtime-tests/lambda/stream-backpressure.test.ts` streams 2 MiB in 16 KiB chunks into a slow writable with a 16 KiB `highWaterMark` and asserts that:

- every byte is written by the time the handler resolves,
- `writableFinished` is `true`,
- the source never runs more than a bounded number of chunks ahead of the sink.

Against `main` the first assertion fails with `expected +0 to be 2097152` — the handler resolves before a single chunk has been flushed.

A second test covers a body that errors mid-stream, confirming the handler still logs and resolves rather than rejecting, so the error contract is unchanged.

Full suite passes: 148 files, 5026 tests.

issue_title: Widen Context<any>'s untyped get/set fallback to accept symbol keys
issue_body:
### What is the feature you are proposing?

`Context<E>`'s untyped fallback (when `E` is `any`, i.e. plain `new Hono()` / `Context` with no `Variables` generic) resolves `get`/`set` to a `Record<string, any>`-keyed shape:

```ts
// context.d.ts
set: Set<IsAny<E> extends true ? {
    Variables: ContextVariableMap & Record<string, any>
    ...
```

`Record<string, any>`'s key type only covers `string | number`, so calling `c.set`/`c.get` with a `symbol` key fails to compile — the same `Argument of type 'unique symbol' is not assignable to parameter of type 'string'` shape as #2484, but for `symbol` instead of a plain string.

The runtime has no such restriction: `set`/`get` store into a `Map` internally, which accepts a `symbol` key without any issue. This is purely a type-level gap, not a real limitation.

**Motivating case:** small frameworks building on top of Hono (mine included — a thin DI/routing layer) often want to stash an internal per-request marker on the context using a `Symbol()` key specifically *because* it can't collide with any string key a user of the framework might set. Today that requires an `as never` cast to work around the type, even though nothing at runtime objects.

**Proposed change:** widen the `IsAny<E>` fallback so it also accepts `symbol` keys, e.g.:

```ts
Variables: ContextVariableMap & Record<string, any> & { [key: symbol]: any }
```

This only changes the *untyped* `Context<any>` branch — anyone using `Hono<{ Variables: {...} }>()` with a concrete `Variables` map is on a different branch of the conditional type and is unaffected, so this shouldn't weaken any existing typed usage.

Happy to open a PR for this if the direction looks right to you.

issue_body:
## Version

hono 4.12.29 and 4.13.1 (latest)

## Expected behavior

A suffix wildcard route like `/assets*` should match `/assets/app.js` regardless of what else is registered on the app.

## Actual behavior

When a mounted sub-app registers a static route and a `:param` route as siblings (same method), every suffix wildcard route (`/assets*`) on the parent app silently returns 404. Slash-star (`/assets/*`) is unaffected.

```ts

const sub = new Hono()

sub.post('/:slug', (c) => c.text('slug'))
app.route('/api', sub)
app.get('/assets*', (c) => c.text('ok'))
console.log((await app.request('http://x/assets/app.js')).status) // 404
```

- Removing either `/items` or `/:slug` makes it work again
- Different methods (`get('/items')` + `post('/:slug')`) is fine
- `{slug}` instead of `:slug` also fixes it
- Confirmed on 4.12.29 and 4.13.1

#4975, #4623 — same router-fallback family, but those cover `/**` with param-vs-param conflicts; this is suffix-`*` with a static-vs-param conflict.

pr_title: perf(jsx/dom): optimize matching-head child lookup during reconciliation
pr_body:
## Problem
During JSX DOM children reconciliation in `hono/jsx/dom/render.ts`, each child in `children` searches `oldVChildren` using `findIndex()` and removes the matched node via `splice()`. When reconciling large child lists where the order is preserved or appended, this produces $O(N^2)$ linear searches and array shift operations.

## Root Cause
Reconciliation did not check the head of `oldVChildren` before falling back to full-array `findIndex()` and `splice()`.

## Fix
Check if `oldVChildren[0]` matches the current child (by string type, key+tag, or tag) and consume it directly via `oldVChildren.shift()`, reducing lookup from $O(N)$ to $O(1)$ for in-order children, while retaining `findIndex()` and `splice()` fallback for reordered or interspersed items.

Related to #5306

1. Added unit test in `src/jsx/dom/index.test.tsx` verifying reconciliation and reordering across 100 keyed items.

This introduces an internal, non-exported `createNullObject()` helper in `src/internal/utils.ts` and uses it for the null-prototype objects created by `RegExpRouter` and `TrieRouter`.

Repeated `Object.create(null)` calls are large enough that sharing them behind a small internal helper produces a clear and measurable reduction in the minified bundle. The helper is internal implementation detail and is not added to Hono's public API.

### Bundle size

Measured with esbuild using `--bundle --minify --format=esm --target=es2022`, compared with the parent branch:

| Entry point | Before | After | Difference |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `src/index.ts` | 18,179 bytes | 17,973 bytes | **-206 bytes** |
| `src/router/reg-exp-router/index.ts` | 6,025 bytes | 5,861 bytes | **-164 bytes** |
| `src/router/trie-router/index.ts` | 2,793 bytes | 2,775 bytes | **-18 bytes** |

The minified-size benefit is concrete, but the runtime trade-off is less universal.

### Runtime considerations

Calling `createNullObject()` introduces a JavaScript function boundary around `Object.create(null)`. A JIT may inline it, but whether and when that happens can depend on the runtime, warm-up state, and call site. Hono supports multiple runtimes, so the result should not be assumed to be identical everywhere.

This PR applies the helper consistently within `RegExpRouter` and `TrieRouter`, including an allocation performed during TrieRouter matching. It does not attempt to replace every `Object.create(null)` in the project, nor does it establish that doing so would always be runtime-neutral.

Future replacements should be evaluated individually, considering:

- the measured minified-size reduction
- whether the call is on an initialization, registration, build, or request-time path
- possible differences between runtimes
- benchmarks when a performance-sensitive path is affected

pr_title: feat(jwt,jwk): add a configurable WWW-Authenticate realm
pr_body:
Refs #4989.

`jwt` and `jwk` build their `401` challenge with the request URL hardcoded as the realm:

```ts
'WWW-Authenticate': `Bearer realm="${opts.ctx.req.url}",error="...",error_description="..."`
```

RFC 6750 describes `realm` as a stable, human-readable name for the protection space. Reflecting the full URL yields a different realm for every path and query string, which is not what the parameter is for:

```
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="https://api.example.com/v1/users/42?token=abc",...
```

`bearer-auth` already exposes a `realm` option. `jwt` and `jwk` had no equivalent, and `unauthorizedResponse()` is private in both, so there was no way to override it short of replacing the middleware.

### Changes

**A `realm` option on both middlewares**, matching `bearer-auth`:

```ts
app.use('/auth/*', jwt({ secret: 'a-secret', alg: 'HS256', realm: 'my-api' }))
// WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="my-api",error="invalid_request",error_description="..."
```

**Quote escaping.** Separately from the realm question, `realm` and `error_description` were interpolated into a quoted-string with no escaping, so a `"` in either truncates the header. Both now get the same `.replace(/"/g, '\\"')` treatment `bearer-auth` applies. This is reachable through the realm option, and `ctx.req.url` is not guaranteed to be percent-encoded on every runtime.

### On the default

The issue proposes defaulting `realm` to `""` instead of `ctx.req.url`. I have **kept the existing default** so this stays non-breaking — anyone relying on the current header sees no change, and the new behavior is opt-in.

Flipping the default is a one-line change (`opts.realm ?? ''`) and I'm happy to make it here if you'd rather correct the default outright — it just seemed like your call rather than mine, so I didn't bundle a behavior change into an additive PR.

issue_title: httpLink / httpBatchLink don't create their own AbortController, so unsubscribe doesn't cancel the request (same pattern as #7389)
issue_body:
#7390 (closing #7389) fixed `httpBatchStreamLink`: it created its own `AbortController` and passed it into `jsonlStreamConsumer`, but the observable's cleanup was a `// noop`, so `abortController.abort()` never ran on unsubscribe and the JSONL stream kept consuming from the server after the subscriber disconnected.

I checked the other HTTP links and this same shape exists in two more:

- `httpLink.ts`: passes `signal: op.signal` straight into `universalRequester`, no internal controller, cleanup is `// noop`.
- `httpBatchLink.ts`: passes `allAbortSignals(...batchOps.map(op => op.signal))`, still only combining caller-provided per-op signals, no internal controller, cleanup is also `// noop`.

Compare with the links that already do this correctly: `httpSubscriptionLink.ts` and `localLink.ts` both do `raceAbortSignals(op.signal, ac.signal)` with their own `ac = new AbortController()`, and call `ac.abort()` in their cleanup. `httpBatchStreamLink.ts` now does the same after #7390.

So `httpLink` and `httpBatchLink` are the two remaining HTTP links that rely entirely on the caller supplying an `op.signal` that happens to fire on unsubscribe, instead of owning their own controller tied to the observable's lifecycle the way every other link in the package does. Whenever the caller's `op.signal` isn't already wired to this specific subscription's teardown, the underlying fetch outlives the subscriber — same wasted-bandwidth/dangling-request consequence as #7389, just without a streamed body to make it as visible in the network tab.
pr_title: fix(client): abort httpLink/httpBatchLink requests on unsubscribe
pr_body:
## What

`httpLink` and `httpBatchLink` rely entirely on the caller-supplied `op.signal` to cancel their in-flight fetch. Their observable cleanup is a `// noop`, so when a subscriber unsubscribes and the caller's `op.signal` isn't wired to that specific subscription's teardown, the underlying `fetch` outlives the subscriber — the same dangling-request/wasted-bandwidth consequence fixed for `httpBatchStreamLink` in #7389 (via #7390).

Every other link in the package (`httpSubscriptionLink`, `localLink`, and `httpBatchStreamLink` after #7390) owns its own `AbortController` and aborts it in cleanup; these two are the remaining holdouts.

## Fix

Mirror #7390's exact pattern in both links:
- `httpLink.ts`: create an `AbortController`, race its signal with `op.signal` via `raceAbortSignals`, and `ac.abort()` in cleanup unless the request already settled.
- `httpBatchLink.ts`: same, with the raced signal fed into the batch loader so the batch fetch's `allAbortSignals` sees it.

Both track an `isDone` flag so a completed/errored request is not spuriously aborted.

## Test

Two regression tests in `packages/tests/server/links.test.ts` (`httpLink - unsubscribe aborts fetch`, `httpBatchLink - unsubscribe aborts fetch`) follow the existing `httpBatchStreamLink` test: they mock `globalThis.fetch`, assert the signal is not aborted before unsubscribe, then assert it is aborted (with an `AbortError` reason) after `sub.unsubscribe()`.

TDD: both tests fail on `main` (cleanup is `// noop`, so the fetch signal never aborts) and pass after the fix.

Fixes #7468

issue_title: WebSocket link silently ignores the operation AbortSignal (removeEventListener with no matching addEventListener)
issue_body:
### Description
An `AbortSignal` passed to a WebSocket operation (`op.signal`, exposed via the `signal` request option) is never wired to anything. Aborting the caller's signal does not cancel an in-flight request nor stop a subscription. This diverges from `httpSubscriptionLink`, which honors `op.signal`.

### Root cause
`packages/client/src/links/wsLink/wsClient/wsClient.ts`: the `request()` teardown calls `signal?.removeEventListener('abort', abort)`, but there is no matching `signal.addEventListener('abort', ...)` anywhere in the `wsLink` client directory (`signal` appears only at the destructure, the type, and the `removeEventListener`; no `signal.aborted`/`throwIfAborted` either). The `removeEventListener` removes a listener that was never added. The v11 refactor (PR #6223) plumbed `signal` into `request()` but only added the cleanup half.

### Steps to reproduce
Subscribe over a WS link with an `AbortController`, then `ac.abort()`. Observed: no `subscription.stop` frame is sent and the subscription keeps running; an in-flight WS query/mutation is likewise not cancelled. Expected: abort tears the operation down (and sends `subscription.stop` for subscriptions).

### Suggested fix
In `request()`, after obtaining `abort`, wire the signal: if `signal?.aborted` tear down immediately; else `signal?.addEventListener('abort', <teardown>, { once: true })`, where teardown calls `abort()`, sends `subscription.stop` for subscriptions, and completes the observer — mirroring the existing return-cleanup.

issue_title: assertIsRequestId is a no-op for all non-number invalid types (only throws for NaN)
issue_body:
### Description
The JSON-RPC request-id validator in the WebSocket message parser is meant to reject anything that isn't `number | string | null`, but its boolean logic only ever throws for `NaN`. Booleans, objects, arrays, and `undefined` all pass as valid request ids and flow downstream into `clientSubscriptions` Map keys and error messages.

### Root cause
`packages/server/src/unstable-core-do-not-import/rpc/parseTRPCMessage.ts`:
```js
if (obj !== null && typeof obj === 'number' && isNaN(obj) && typeof obj !== 'string') {
  throw new Error('Invalid request id');
}
```
`typeof obj === 'number'` combined with `typeof obj !== 'string'` (always true once the former holds) plus `isNaN(obj)` means the throw fires only for `NaN`. Git history shows the original (PR #508) was correct -- `if (typeof obj !== 'number' || isNaN(obj))` -- and the boolean got inverted when the type was widened to `number | string | null`.

### Steps to reproduce
```
NaN          -> throws (correct)
true         -> passes (should throw)
{}           -> passes (should throw)
[]           -> passes (should throw)
undefined    -> passes (should throw)

pr_title: fix(server): correct assertIsRequestId boolean logic — non-NaN invalid types passed silently
pr_body:
## Summary

`assertIsRequestId` in `parseTRPCMessage.ts` has an inverted boolean condition that only throws for `NaN`. Booleans, objects, arrays, and `undefined` all pass through silently as valid request IDs.

**Root cause**

```ts
// Before — broken: only throws when typeof obj === 'number' AND isNaN(obj)
if (
  obj !== null &&
  typeof obj === 'number' &&   // short-circuits for non-numbers
  isNaN(obj) &&
  typeof obj !== 'string'      // always true when typeof obj === 'number'
) {
  throw new Error('Invalid request id');
}
```

The original intent (PR #508) was `typeof id !== 'number' || isNaN(id)`. The condition got inverted when the type was widened to `number | string | null`.

**Fix**

```ts
// After — throws for anything that is not null, a finite number, or a string
if (
  obj !== null &&
  typeof obj !== 'string' &&
  (typeof obj !== 'number' || isNaN(obj))
) {
  throw new Error('Invalid request id');
}
```

## Previously broken (now fixed)

| Input | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `NaN` | throws | throws |
| `true` | passes silently | throws |
| `false` | passes silently | throws |
| `{}` | passes silently | throws |
| `[]` | passes silently | throws |
| `undefined` | passes silently | throws |

## Tests

Added 11 unit tests in `packages/tests/server/parseTRPCMessage.test.ts` covering all valid (`number`, `string`, `null`, `0`, `""`) and all previously-silent-invalid cases.

Fixes #7430, fixes #7450

**File:** `packages/client/src/links/httpBatchStreamLink.ts` (lines 75, 139, 216)
**Version:** v11.17.0

### Describe the bug

In `httpBatchStreamLink`, an `AbortController` is created and passed to `jsonlStreamConsumer` to signal cancellation of the JSONL response stream. However, the observable's cleanup function is a noop:

  // noop

4. Open DevTools → Network tab

issue_title: bug(server): handle React 19 proxy coercion in createInnerProxy
pr_title: fix(server): handle React 19 proxy coercion in createInnerProxy
pr_body:
## Problem

React 19 can coerce a proxy object to a primitive by calling `valueOf()`, `toString()`, or `toJSON()` on it — for example during rendering, string interpolation, or console logging. When these methods are called on the proxy returned by `createInnerProxy()`, the current `get` trap simply returns *another proxy*, which:

- breaks any consumer that expects a primitive back
- can cause infinite recursion in coercion-heavy paths
- requires downstream apps to carry a `patch-package` workaround across every `@11.x` upgrade

Related React upstream issue: https://github.com/facebook/react/issues/35657

## Fix

Add an early-return guard in the `get` trap for the three coercion keys:

```ts
if (key === 'valueOf' || key === 'toString' || key === 'toJSON') {
  const debugPath = path.join('.');
  return () => `tRPC.proxy(${debugPath})`;
}
```

The returned function yields a debug string (`tRPC.proxy(foo.bar)`) which:
- satisfies any caller trying to coerce the proxy to a string or number
- follows the same convention the issue author used in their local patch
- does not change any existing behavior (normal chaining continues to work)

## Tests

Added a dedicated test case `createRecursiveProxy() - handles React 19 proxy coercion keys` that verifies:
- `valueOf`, `toString`, and `toJSON` each return a *function* (not a proxy)
- calling those functions returns the correct debug string
- normal proxy chaining still produces the expected callback invocation after those keys exist on the object

Closes #7335
